'''''Epiphyllum oxypetalum''''', the '''Dutchman's pipe cactus''',<ref name=GRIN>{{citation |url=https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxonomydetail.aspx?id=27844 |title=USDA GRIN Taxonomy |accessdate=6 August 2016}}</ref> '''princess of the night''' or '''queen of the night''',<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.beyondsciencetv.com/2018/05/23/queen-of-the-night-the-flower-that-only-blooms-one-night-a-year/ |date=May 23, 2018 |title=Queen of the Night: The Flower That Only Blooms ONE Night A Year - Beyond Science TV |website=beyondsciencetv.com |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190410141705/https://www.beyondsciencetv.com/2018/05/23/queen-of-the-night-the-flower-that-only-blooms-one-night-a-year/ |access-date=28 December 2018|archive-date=10 April 2019 }}</ref> is a species of [[cactus]] with a native range from Mexico to Nicaragua.<ref>{{Cite POWO |title=''Epiphyllum oxypetalum'' (DC.) Haw. |id=132938-1 |access-date=2023-12-23}}</ref> It blooms nocturnally, and its flowers wilt before dawn. Though it is sometimes referred to as a [[night-blooming cereus]], it is not closely related to any of the species in the tribe [[Cereeae]] that are more commonly known by that name. All ''Cereus'' species bloom at night and are terrestrial plants; ''Epiphyllum'' species are usually [[epiphytic]].

==Description==
The stems are erect, ascending, [[scandent]], or sprawling and profusely branched. The primary stems are [[terete]], up to {{convert|6|m}} long, flattened laterally, and ligneous at their bases. The secondary stems are flat, elliptic-acuminate, up to {{cvt|30|x|12|cm|in|0}}. The stem margins are shallowly through deeply crenate and undulate. Stems appear to be waxy therefore cutin may be present. Cutin reduces water loss from stems. A gel-like substance oozes out of stem cuts. Stems contain much water-filled tissue.{{cn|date=August 2026}}

===Flowers===
The flowers are nocturnal. They grow on flattened stems and are up to {{cvt|30|cm|in|0}} long and {{cvt|17|cm|in|0}} wide, and very fragrant. The principal odor components in the aroma are [[benzyl salicylate]] and methyl linoleate.<ref name="Lim2014">{{cite book | last1 = Lim | first1 = T. K. | title = Edible Medicinal and Non-Medicinal Plants | chapter = Epiphyllum oxypetalum | date = 2014 | pages = 638–640 | doi = 10.1007/978-94-007-7395-0_43 | isbn = 978-94-007-7394-3 }}</ref> [[Pericarpel]]s are nude, slightly angled, and green. [[Bracteole]]s are short and narrow up through ca. {{cvt|10|mm}} long. Receptacles are up through {{cvt|20|cm|0}} long, {{cvt|1|cm|1}} thick, brownish, and arching. The outer [[tepal]]s are linear, acute, {{cvt|8–10|cm}} long, and reddish through amber. The inner tepals are whitish, oblanceolate or oblong, acuminate, up through 8–10 cm long and {{cvt|2.5|cm}} wide. The [[stamen]]s are greenish white or white, slender and weak. The [[Style (botany)|styles]] are greenish white, pale yellow, or white, {{cvt|4|mm}} thick, as long as inner tepals, and with many lobes.{{cn|date=August 2026}}

The fruits are oblong, up through 12 x 8 cm, purplish red, and angled.{{cn|date=August 2026}}

==Systematics==
This species is closely related to ''[[Epiphyllum thomasianum|E. thomasianum]]'' and ''[[Epiphyllum pumilum|E. pumilum]]'', but quite distinct from them.{{citation needed|date=August 2016}} In 1909, C. A. Purpus collected a slightly different type in St. Ana, Orizaba, Mexico. It has carmine red outer petals and the flowers have an unpleasant smell, rather than being fragrant. It was originally named ''Phyllocactus purpusii'', but is now included within this species.{{cn|date=August 2026}}

==Range==
''Epiphyllum oxypetalum'' is native to Southern Mexico and to extensive areas of South America.<ref name=GRIN /> It is widely cultivated, with many [[escaped plant|escapes from cultivation]] in tropical areas, especially in southeast Asia.<ref>{{citation |chapter-url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200014503 |title=Flora of China |chapter=''Epiphyllum oxypetalum'' (Candolle) Haworth, Phil. Mag. Ann. Chem. 6: 109. 1829 |first1=Zhen-yu |last1=Li |first2=Nigel P. |last2=Taylor }}</ref> It has become [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] in China.<ref name=GRIN />

==Cultivation and uses==
''Epiphyllum oxypetalum'' is an easily cultivated, fast growing ''Epiphyllum''. It flowers in late spring through late summer; large specimens can produce several crops of flowers in one season. This is a widely cultivated ''Epiphyllum'' species.{{cn|date=August 2026}}

It is known to have medicinal properties in many Asian cultures, including India, Vietnam, and Malaysia. The plant is widely used in traditional medicine to treat respiratory ailments, bleeding conditions, and is also believed to have the property of reducing pain and inflammation.{{citation needed|date=June 2021}}

In the popular movie ''[[Crazy Rich Asians]]'', based on the novel by Kevin Kwan, the characters organise  parties to watch the brief blooming of the plant known in Chinese as ''tan hua'' ''({{lang-zh|t=曇花|s=昙花|p=tánhuā}}).''<ref>{{cite journal |last=Sio |first=Joanna Ut-Seong |date=2019-07-03 |title=Crazy Rich Asians (2018) |journal=Asian Ethnicity |volume=20 |issue=3 |pages=393–395 |doi=10.1080/14631369.2018.1559035 |issn=1463-1369}}</ref>
